identity.title: Which Algorithms Can Graph Neural Networks Learn?

problem.claim: Determine when message-passing graph neural networks (MPNNs) can learn to execute discrete algorithms and generalize from small training instances to inputs of arbitrary size.

gap.claim: Existing work is described as mainly empirical without formal guarantees or focused only on expressivity, leaving generalization beyond finite training sets unresolved.

contributions.claim: A framework giving sufficient conditions for MPNNs to learn algorithms from small instances and provably approximate their behavior on arbitrary-size inputs with worst-case guarantees.
Impossibility results for tasks that standard MPNNs cannot learn, together with more expressive MPNN-like architectures intended to overcome those limitations.
A refined Bellman–Ford analysis with substantially smaller required training sets and a differentiable regularization loss, extending the cited recent work.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors state a general theoretical framework combining sufficient conditions and worst-case arbitrary-size guarantees, plus impossibility results and corresponding more expressive architectures.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The framework applies to single-source shortest paths, minimum spanning trees, and dynamic programming problems including 0–1 knapsack.
The Bellman–Ford refinement reportedly reduces required training-set size substantially and permits a differentiable regularization loss relative to Nerem et al., 2025.
Empirical results are reported to largely support the theoretical findings.

narrative_sequence.summary: The paper situates neural algorithmic reasoning in efforts to integrate discrete algorithm execution into larger neural pipelines, highlighting MPNNs and a lack of formal generalization guarantees.
It proposes sufficient conditions for learning algorithms from small instances while guaranteeing worst-case approximation on arbitrary-size inputs, across several algorithm families.
It reports standard-MPNN impossibility results, proposes more expressive variants, and specializes the analysis to Bellman–Ford with smaller training sets and differentiable regularization.
The abstract reports that experiments largely support the theory.

source_observation.claim: The abstract aligns broad positive applicability claims with explicit worst-case guarantees, then separately states impossibility results and architectural remedies.

lessons.interpretation: A useful research narrative distinguishes sufficient conditions from fundamental limitations instead of presenting a method as universally capable.
lessons.application: Frame a theory paper around a capability boundary: state the conditions for success, identify tasks excluded by the baseline, and specify what added expressivity addresses them.
lessons.exception: This framing may be unsuitable when the work does not establish formal conditions or task-specific limitations.

unknowns: The abstract does not state the sufficient conditions, guarantee form, approximation metric, or required training-set sizes.
The impossibility task range and the exact architecture changes are unspecified.
Empirical datasets, metrics, baselines, and the meaning of “largely support” are not reported.
